title: Why Before School Is The Perfect Time To Build Rapport https://smartclassroommanagement.com/2012/06/09/building-rapport-with-students-before-school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin makes the case that the few minutes before the morning bell are an ideal, underused opportunity for teachers to build rapport with students. Rather than staying at their desks finishing preparations, he urges teachers to go to wherever students gather before school and simply spend unstructured, no-agenda time chatting and listening. He outlines several specific benefits: it's an easy, organic way to build rapport, it creates opportunities to connect with quieter students, it demonstrates that each day is a fresh start, and it draws less popular students into the social fold. He closes by warning that trying too hard undermines the effort, and that authentic rapport comes from being relaxed, listening more than talking, and simply being oneself.
points: Spending five minutes with students before school builds behavior-influencing rapport and leverage more efficiently than almost any in-class strategy.
Effective before-school connection requires no agenda or expectations — just presence, listening, and genuine interest.
Casual morning time is especially valuable for drawing out shy or quieter students who may not otherwise open up in class.
Before-school interactions help prove to skeptical or difficult students that each day is a fresh start, reinforcing a core turnaround strategy.
The biggest rapport-building mistake is trying too hard — dominating conversation, over-praising, or forcing interactions rather than letting them happen naturally.
quotes: Because having rapport with students translates to powerful and behavior-influencing leverage—the kind of leverage that compels them to want to behave, to want to do well, and to want to please you.
Simply being with your students outside the limits of the classroom is an easy, organic way to build rapport.
The idea that yesterday’s mistakes and misbehaviors are forgotten is an important part of an overall strategy to turn around your most difficult students.
The biggest mistake teachers make when attempting to build rapport is that they try too hard. They dominate the conversation—talking at, rather than with, students.
The truth is, having a healthy, trusting, and influential rapport with students, the kind that gives your classroom management plan relevance and meaning, is primarily a function of your likeability.
Listen more than talk. Don’t try so hard. Let the conversation come to you—and then let it go where it goes.
